title: Data Management
overview: Choose datastores from the workload: required queries, write volume, consistency, availability, latency and schema evolution. This topic compares replication, sharding and caching, explains CAP during network partitions, then surveys key-value, document, wide-column, search, graph and SQL-over-files models. Treat named products as lecture examples rather than guarantees of every deployment.
big_ideas: RDBMS fits many workloads; horizontal distribution, schema evolution and relationship traversals can motivate other models.
Read replicas distribute reads; shards divide data and write load; caches reduce repeated reads, while write durability depends on the acknowledgement path.
CAP is a trade-off during partitions: preserve consistent answers by refusing some requests, or keep answering while accepting divergent data.
The lecture labels Redis, MongoDB and HBase CP and Elasticsearch AP; reason from partition behaviour and configuration rather than the product name alone.
CQRS separates command and query models; the lecture illustrates independently scaled databases with asynchronous projections.
Choose key-value for point lookup, document for nested data, wide-column for sparse write-heavy records, search for ranked retrieval and graph for traversals.
SQL-over-files separates query processing from stored files. Do not infer that every named analytics product lacks managed database capabilities.

sections.title: What we need from a datastore and where RDBMS stands
sections.summary: Datastore requirements (scale, consistency, availability, latency, evolvability) and an honest assessment of RDBMS against them.

notes.lead: Applications are built to be **available, fault-tolerant, performant and gracefully degrading**, so datastores must be too, while coping with **IoT and analytics-driven data volume**.
items: Beyond storing and reading data, we want:
**Structured** → follows a defined model, such as relational rows and columns
**Semi-structured** → carries labels or hierarchy, such as **JSON** or **XML**
**CSV** → the lecture also groups it as semi-structured; a fixed CSV table can be treated as structured
**Unstructured** → content such as images or prose; lacks a predefined application-level record model

notes.h: RDBMS is great for most scenarios
items: **Entities map to tables**
**SQL**
**Flexible querying on any column**
**Logical data model**
**Good read/write performance**
**Strong ACID consistency**
**Scaling across machines** while keeping strong consistency requires coordination
**Schema changes need planning**
**Object models must map to tables**, sometimes through an **ORM**
An **ORM is optional**, not a relational requirement
**Deep relationship traversal** can favour a **graph model**, depending on the query

terms.def: Defined model of rows and columns with strict schema.
Labelled or hierarchical records, such as JSON or XML, without a fixed relational table layout.
Content without a predefined application-level record model, such as prose or images.

check.q: A platform's domain model changes almost weekly, and every change needs a table migration and an update to the object-relational mapping. Which datastore requirement is the relational database weakest on here, and what would you consider?

items: **Strict schema** → has to be **migrated**
Domain entities must be translated to tables through an **ORM**
**Consider a schema-free document store** → smoother **schema evolution**, because the schema travels with the data
a.foot: **Trade-off**: most document stores give up **joins, constraints and complex transactions** → switch only if those matter less than the **pace of change**.

check.q: A teammate says: 'Relational databases don't scale, so our 2,000-user internal app needs NoSQL.' Do you agree?

items: The lecture says an **RDBMS is great for most scenarios**: flexible **SQL on any column**, strong **ACID** guarantees, good **read and write performance**
**What is hard**: **scaling horizontally while staying consistent** → **replication and sharding** exist for that
**2,000 users** rarely need it
a.foot: Reach for another model when a **specific need** appears, such as **graph-like relationships**, very **high write volume** or constant **schema change**.

check.q: A platform stores invoices as rows, partner webhook payloads as JSON, and scanned receipts as images. Classify each kind of data and say what it implies for storage.

items: **Invoices** → **structured** data with a strict schema → **relational tables**
**Webhook payloads** → **semi-structured**, schema attached to the data → **document store** or a **JSON column**
**Scanned receipts** → **unstructured** → store as **files or objects**, keep their metadata in a **queryable store**
a.foot: One platform therefore often needs **more than one kind of store**.

sections.title: Scaling databases: replication, sharding, caching
sections.summary: Use replicas to distribute reads, shards to divide the dataset and caches for hot data. Separate read caching from the durability policy for writes.

items: **Only the master accepts writes**
**Read replicas** → full read-only copies
Clients are **routed to any replica** for reads
If a **replica is down, others serve**
**Small replication lag** → reads can be slightly stale
**Shard** → a subset of data (**horizontal partitioning**)
**One master per shard**, partitioned across machines
**Locator service** → tells clients which master owns which shard
**Algorithm sits in the client**, like a **HashMap**
**Fixed sharding key** → may distribute poorly
**Hash-based partitioning** → distributes more evenly
If **shards change**, masters **publish events**
**Read-through** → fetches from the database on a cache miss
**Write-through** → acknowledge only after the backing store has accepted the write under its **durability policy**
**Write-behind** (delayed flushing) → acknowledging an in-memory write first **risks data loss** if the cache fails
notes.foot: The lecture mentions both durability and pre-flush loss; **distinguish the acknowledgement timing**.

terms.def: Read-only copy of the full dataset.
A subset of the data with its own master.
Tells clients which shard master owns which data.
Write via the cache to the backing store before acknowledging success; durability depends on that store’s guarantee.

check.q: Writes saturate the primary database at peak, so the team adds three more read replicas. What effect will this have?

items: **Replicas** are **read-only copies**; every write still goes to the **single master**
**To spread writes, shard** the data → each shard has its **own master** → improves both **write and read** throughput
a.foot: **Sharding costs** routing, either a **locator service** or a **client-side algorithm**, and makes **queries across shards** harder.

check.q: Orders are sharded by country, and 70% of orders come from one country. What happens, and what would you change?

a.lead: **That shard's master becomes a hot spot** while the others sit idle.
items: **Cause**: a **fixed sharding key** does not distribute data evenly
**Change**: **hash-based partitioning** on a **high-cardinality key** such as order ID → spreads load more evenly
With **algorithmic sharding**, the client computes the shard **without a locator**
a.foot: **Cost**: you lose **locality**, since one country's orders are now spread across shards, and **shard changes must be announced** to clients.

check.q: A cache in front of the database acknowledges writes from memory and flushes them to disk every 30 seconds. Is that acceptable for payments? For page-view counters?

sub: If the cache fails before flushing → **acknowledged payments are lost**
Use **write-through**: acknowledges only after the **backing store** has the write
Losing a few seconds of counts is usually acceptable
**Delayed persistence** can buy the speed of **in-memory writes**

check.q: Reads are routed to replicas. After updating their profile, some users see the old version on the next page load. Diagnose the problem and suggest fixes.

a.lead: **Replication lag**: the write reached the master, but the replica serving the next read has not caught up.
items: **Fix**: route a user's reads to the **master** for a short time **after they write**
**Fix**: read **critical views** from the master
a.foot: Either way the **master takes more read load**, so accept lag wherever stale data is harmless.

visuals.title: Scaling techniques
rows: Master takes writes; replicas serve reads
One master per subset of data; locator or algorithm
Read-through on miss; choose write policy
Acknowledged but unflushed writes can be lost

sections.title: CAP: consistency vs availability
sections.summary: CAP constrains behaviour during a network partition. Decide whether refusing some operations or serving potentially inconsistent data is acceptable for the business.

items: **Consistency** → operations behave as if using **one current copy**
**Availability** → requests to **non-failing nodes receive results** rather than being refused to preserve consistency
**Partition tolerance** → accounts for **network links failing** between nodes
notes.foot: **During a partition**, a distributed system cannot guarantee **both C and A** for all operations.

items: **CP** → reject or delay operations that cannot be answered consistently
**AP** → keep accepting operations on separated nodes, allowing **divergence** and later **reconciliation**
notes.foot: **Outside a partition**, CAP does not require choosing only consistency or availability.

items: **Master-only read path** → illustrates a **CP choice** when an isolated node cannot serve inconsistent data or take over unsafely
**Read routing alone is not proof**: failover, replication and write acknowledgement also matter
A **stale replica read alone** does not establish full **AP** availability
**Stale feed or cart** → may be preferable to no service
**Payment balance** → may justify refusing an unsafe operation
**Make the choice per operation**, then check the implementation
notes.foot: A **convenient data model does not determine CAP behaviour**.

terms.def: During a network partition a store must choose consistency or availability.
Keeps consistency, may refuse some requests.
Stays available, may return stale reads (eventual consistency).

check.q: A shopping cart is replicated across two regions, and the network between them fails. Should the cart stay available or refuse changes?

items: A slightly **stale or diverging cart** is better than **no cart**
The lecture's point: this is a **business decision** more than a technical one
**Cost**: **reconciling** the diverged copies when the partition heals
**Risk**: a user briefly sees an **old cart**
a.foot: **Checkout**, which takes money, may still need a stricter rule.

check.q: A payments ledger is replicated across two data centres, and the link between them fails. What should the system do?

items: **Refuse or delay** the operations that cannot be applied consistently, such as **debits** on the side that cannot reach the **authoritative copy**
→ Rather than risk **double-spending**
Some customers get **errors** during the partition, which the business accepts as the **lesser harm** for money
**Reads of the balance** may also be refused or marked as **possibly stale**

check.q: The lecture's shortcut says that if reads go to the master only, the system is CP. What must you check before relying on that?

items: Can an **isolated old master** still **accept writes**?
How does **failover** choose a new master?
When are writes **acknowledged** relative to **replication**?
a.foot: If failover can **promote a replica that missed acknowledged writes**, the system is not as consistent as the shortcut suggests: **master-only reads** are the lecture's simplified illustration, not a full guarantee.

check.q: A teammate says their single-node database avoids the CAP trade-off entirely. How do you respond?

items: A **single instance** is not a distributed system → **CAP does not apply**
But it is also a **single point of failure**
The lecture says **distributed datastores must tolerate partitions** → once you add a **replica** for availability or scale, you must choose **consistency or availability** for partition time
a.foot: The single node has avoided the choice by **giving up availability** whenever it fails.

visuals.title: CP vs AP
rows: May reject requests to preserve consistency
visuals.caption: Product labels below reproduce the lecture’s examples. Actual guarantees depend on replication, failover and operation settings.

sections.title: Why NoSQL and polyglot data models
sections.summary: Platforms have unique, changing requirements, so they use several databases, and NoSQL fills the gaps RDBMS leaves.

items: **Write-heavy**
**Read-heavy**
**Analytics-based consumption**
**Varied query patterns**
**Scalability/availability needs**
**Schema changes are the norm** in fast-moving platforms

notes.lead: Separate the model **accepting commands** from the model **serving queries**.
items: The two sides **scale independently**
**Asynchronous projection** → reads can **lag writes**
CQRS **does not inherently require** all these components
**Can improve scale or latency** via partitioning, replication, flexible records, workload-specific indexes
**Transaction scope, consistency and durability vary** by store and configuration
**Flexible schema** does not remove the need to **validate records** or evolve their meaning
**Key-value**
**Document**
**Column family** (wide column)
**Search engines**
**Graph**

terms.def: Separating the write model from the read model so each scales independently.

check.q: In the lecture's CQRS design, a command succeeds but the next query still shows the old value. Is that necessarily a failed write?

items: The command commits to the **write store**
The **read database** is updated **asynchronously** from **published events** → the query can run before the **projection** catches up
Check **event delivery** and **projection progress** before suspecting the write
a.foot: This **lag** is the price of **scaling reads and writes independently**.

check.q: To reduce operational cost, an architect wants one database technology for the whole platform. The platform has a write-heavy telemetry feed, a product catalogue whose attributes change often, and a social graph. How do you respond?

items: **Telemetry**: **write-heavy** and **sparse**
**Catalogue**: needs **schema flexibility** and **rich queries**
**Social graph**: about **traversing relationships**
The lecture notes that **most modern platforms use multiple databases** for exactly this reason
a.foot: The architect's concern is real, since **every extra store adds operations work** → add a store only where the workload clearly needs it.

check.q: Order history is read about 100 times for every write, while writes need strict validation. Would CQRS help, and what would it cost?

items: **Commands** → a **write API** with full **validation** → the **write store**
**Events** are projected into a **read model** shaped for the history screens
**Read APIs** scale **independently** of writes
**Cost**: the **lag** between a write and its appearance in the read model, plus the work of running the **event flow and projections**
a.foot: If users must see their **own change immediately**, serve that view from the **write side**.

steps.label: Write API
steps.detail: Writes to the RDBMS and publishes events.

steps.label: RDBMS + event store
steps.detail: RDBMS holds the transactional data; the event store receives published events.

steps.label: Subscribe & project
steps.detail: Events are projected into an in-memory database.

steps.label: Read APIs
steps.detail: Reads come from the in-memory database and can be scaled independently of writes.

sections.title: Key-value stores
sections.summary: The lecture’s hash-map model makes exact-key lookup cheap; arbitrary field and range queries need additional indexing or a different model.

items: Given a key, **fetch the whole record as fast as possible** (in memory)
Roughly a **distributed HashMap** with **unique keys** replicated across servers
**Strength** → a hash-style key lookup is fast
**Limit** → does not automatically provide **ordered range scans** or **queries on value fields**
Lecture emphasises **in-memory stores** → their **capacity and persistence policy** affect cost and durability
Those traits should **not be assumed for every key-value implementation**
**In-memory store** with **richer data structures**
Illustrated with reads and writes through **one shard master**
Labelled **CP**
Preserve that example, but **check actual partition and failover behaviour** before claiming consistent failover or no data loss

terms.def: Lookup of one record by its exact key.

check.q: Shopping carts are kept in a key-value store for fast lookup by cart ID. A product team now wants 'all carts updated in the last hour' from the same store. Advise.

items: **Key-value stores** are built for **point queries by key**; **range queries** are expensive by design → this would mean **scanning everything**
**Instead**: publish cart updates to a **store or index** built for that query, or maintain a separate **time-ordered index**
Keep the key-value store for what it does best

check.q: A team plans to keep two terabytes of rarely read historical records in an in-memory key-value store because lookups are fast. What would you point out?

items: Most key-value stores keep **everything in memory** and **flush to disk** occasionally → need **large amounts of memory**, and **persistence affects performance**
Paying for memory to hold **cold data** wastes the store's strength
**Keep hot data** there, such as **carts, sessions and rate-limit counters**
Move **historical records** to a **cheaper store** suited to infrequent reads

check.q: The lecture's key-value architecture sends all reads and writes for a key through its shard's master and labels it CP. What does that mean during a partition, and what should you still verify?

items: **During a partition**: if a shard's **master is unreachable**, its keys are **unavailable until failover**, rather than being served stale from a replica
**Verify** how **failover** works and when writes are **acknowledged**: promoting a replica that missed recent writes can **lose acknowledged data**
a.foot: The **CP label** describes the illustrated design, not every configuration of every product.

sections.title: Document stores
sections.summary: Embed related records in JSON documents to avoid some joins. Evaluate query indexes, transaction scope and validation needs for the chosen store.

items: **Richer querying on all fields** without the limits of a strict schema

sub: eBay search suggestions and product catalogue

items: **Nest related child data inside a parent document** → for example an order with line items
So **one fetch** can return it
**Flexible fields ease evolution**
But old and new record shapes still need **validation** and **compatible readers**
**Field indexes** support rich queries
**Embedding avoids many joins**
**MongoDB has some join support**
notes.foot: These are comparison points to **verify for the chosen product**, not universal absences across document stores.

items: **JSON-style CRUD**
**Master-based architecture**, labelled **CP**
Use that as the illustrated configuration; consistency still depends on **replication, failover and operation settings**

terms.def: Nesting child entities inside the parent document.

check.q: An order, its line items and its shipping address are always read and written together, and the attributes vary by product type. Document or relational store?

items: **Embed** the line items and address in the order document → one **id-based fetch** returns everything
The **schema-free** model handles **varying attributes**
Works because the order is the **natural unit of reading and writing**
a.foot: The **relational model** would fit better if line items were **updated independently** by many processes, or reporting needed **joins** across orders and products.

check.q: A team wants to move its accounting system, which depends on joins, constraints and triggers, to a document store for schema flexibility. Advise.

items: The lecture warns most document stores lack **joins, complex transactions, SQL, constraints and triggers**
Accounting relies on exactly those to protect **integrity**
**Schema flexibility** does not justify losing those guarantees
a.foot: A document store could still serve a **derived, read-only view** if some screens need flexible documents.

sections.title: Column family (wide column) stores
sections.summary: Write-heavy, sparse, massively scalable nested maps keyed by row key, column key and timestamp.

items: **Write-heavy workloads** (tens of thousands of records a second)
**Very flexible and sparse schema**
**Fetch an entire record by key**

sub: Facebook inbox search and messenger (Cassandra then HBase)

items: A **distributed nested map** indexed by **row key**, **column family/qualifier** and a **timestamp version**
**Rows may have different columns**
This is the **HBase-style example** → use its keys to reason about retrieval, rather than assuming all wide-column products expose an identical key model
**Sparse rows and partitioned storage** suit high write volume
**Plan queries around the row key**
**Joins** are not the normal access path; **secondary indexes** may be costly
**SQL-like interfaces** (lecture) → **CQL** for Cassandra, **Phoenix** over HBase
Scale still depends on **partition balance** and **query shape**
Each **region owned by a single server**
**Replication via HDFS** (typically **3 replicas**)
A **CP** system

terms.def: Group of related columns; column key = family.qualifier.
Another name for column-family store; columns can vary per row.

check.q: A fleet of sensors sends 50,000 readings a second, each sensor reporting a different, sparse set of fields. The main query is 'all readings for sensor X over a time range'. Which data model fits, and how would you design the key?

items: **Linearly scalable**, handles **very high write volumes**
Lets each row have a **different set of columns**
Design the **row key** around the query, e.g. **sensor ID plus time** → one sensor's range is read **contiguously**
The key must **spread writes across shards** → avoid keys where all current writes land on **one region**

check.q: Later, analysts want 'every sensor whose temperature ever exceeded 80' across the whole fleet. What happens with the wide-column design, and what would you do?

items: Nothing in the **row key** supports that query → it needs a **full scan** or a **secondary index**, which the lecture says is **significantly slower and expensive**
A wide-column store is **not a general-purpose database**, and there are **no joins**
**Do**: copy the data into an **analytics engine**, such as **SQL over files**, or a store designed for that query

sections.title: Search engines
sections.summary: Elasticsearch-style stores for ranking, range, wildcard, filtering and aggregations, not as a primary store.

sub: Netflix service operations and security logs

notes.h: Use as a derived search index
items: **Tokenisation, analysis and index maintenance** add write cost
Lecture warns against relying on it for **relational-style joins and transactions**
**Keep authoritative** payment/order data elsewhere; **rebuild the searchable view** from that source
**Data nodes** → hold searchable data
**Master** → manages cluster-wide metadata, node membership and shard allocation
Lecture labels **Elasticsearch AP**
That shorthand **does not guarantee every request succeeds** during every failure → analyse the concrete topology and operation

terms.def: Splitting text into searchable terms during indexing, which slows insertion.

check.q: A team proposes writing orders only to the search engine, since it already powers order search and returns results quickly. Do you agree?

a.lead: **No.** The lecture says search engines are **not recommended as a primary datastore**.
items: **Insertions are slow** because of **tokenisation and analysis**
**No joins or transactions**
Keep orders in a **transactional system of record** and **derive the search index** from it
Accept a **short delay** before new orders become searchable
a.foot: The index can then be **rebuilt from the source** if it is lost or corrupted.

check.q: Product search needs ranking, wildcards, filters and aggregations over ten million products, whose source of truth is a document store. Design the data flow, and say where search results must not be trusted.

items: **Data flow**: publish product changes from the **system of record** → an **indexer** updates the **search engine**
**Ranking, wildcard, range and filter** queries run there
The lecture's search architecture is **AP** → results can be **briefly stale or inconsistent**
a.foot: Fine for **browsing**, but **stock levels and prices at checkout** must be read from the system of record.

sections.title: Graph stores, SQL over files, and choosing
sections.summary: Use graph models when traversing relationships is central. SQL-over-files engines provide a query layer over externally stored analytical data.

notes.h: Graph stores: relationships are the point
items: **Example** → Neo4j
**Traversals crossing machine boundaries** add coordination and network cost → **partitioning is difficult**
**Broad aggregations** can require large scans; not every aggregation necessarily visits every node
**Choose by** traversal shape, dataset and distribution needs
Lecture groups **Hive, Athena, BigQuery and Snowflake**
They do **SQL parsing, job generation and metadata management** over files
Learn the **separation of query compute from stored data**
The broad label **"not a database"** is a teaching simplification, not a reliable classification of every listed analytics product
**Key-value** → fastest key lookup (carts, sessions, caches)
**Document** → rich querying with flexible schema
**Column family** → write-heavy sparse data at massive scale
**Search engine** → advanced search and logs
**Graph** → relationships
**SQL-over-files** → analytics on stored files

terms.def: Stores entities and relationships and answers connection queries by traversal.
Engines like Hive/Athena that run SQL on files via parser, job generator and metadata manager.

check.q: A venture-capital firm wants to find investors who co-invest with investors who co-invested with investor X, three hops out. Which data model fits, and what are its limits?

items: The question is about **relationships between things** → **traversing a few hops** is natural there, whereas **relational joins three levels deep** get expensive
**Limit**: **horizontal scaling is hard**, because splitting a graph across machines needs costly **coordination**
**Limit**: **aggregations** require traversing the **entire database**
a.foot: Keep it for **relationship queries** and do the totals elsewhere.

check.q: Analysts want ad hoc SQL over five years of log files already sitting in file or object storage, a few times a week. Would you load them into a relational database or use a SQL-over-files engine?

items: Not a database but a **SQL parser, job generator and metadata manager** over the existing files → nothing has to be loaded or managed in tables
Suits **occasional analytical queries** over **large data**
a.foot: **Trade-off**: individual queries are **slower** than on an indexed transactional database, and it does not manage **transactional records**, so it is not a replacement for the application's store.

visuals.title: NoSQL models at a glance
rows: Fast point lookup: carts, cache, sessions
Embedding and transaction boundaries need care
Indexing cost; not a relational transaction store
visuals.caption: CAP labels are the lecture’s simplified architecture examples; choose guarantees separately from the data model.

exam_angles.q: A global shopping app needs a cart, a product catalogue with varied attributes, order history with financial integrity, product search, and 'customers also bought' recommendations. Choose a data model for each, justify it, and name the main cost of the overall design.

items: **Cart → key-value store**: fast lookup by **cart ID**, replicated and kept **available during partitions**, since a stale cart beats no cart
**Catalogue → document store**: nested, **varying product attributes** fit **schema-free** documents
**Orders → relational store**: **ACID transactions** and **constraints**
**Search → search engine index** derived from the catalogue, **never the primary store**
**Recommendations → graph store**: traverse **customer-product relationships**
a.foot: **Main cost: operational**: five stores to run, plus the **event flows** that keep the derived ones in step → drop any store whose workload does not justify it.

exam_angles.q: Using CAP, decide how (a) a social media timeline and (b) a payments ledger should behave during a network partition between data centres, and explain why the decision is a business one.

a.lead: During a partition a distributed store must choose: keep answering and risk stale or divergent data (**AP**), or refuse some operations to stay consistent (**CP**).
items: **(a) Timeline → stay available**: some posts are better than none, and **stale feeds** are a minor annoyance
**(b) Ledger → prefer consistency**: reject **debits** it cannot apply safely, because a **wrong balance** costs far more than a **temporary error**
**Business decision**: the question is **which harm** users and the company can tolerate, not which technology is better

exam_angles.q: A ticketing platform must accept 60,000 seat purchases in the first two minutes of a sale. The database has one primary and one read replica, and performance tests show write throughput is the bottleneck. Propose a plan to scale writes, including the changes to software, and identify two side effects to monitor.

a.lead: **Replicas cannot help**, because all writes go to the one primary.
items: **Shard the seat inventory**, e.g. by **hash of event and seat block** → each shard has its **own master**
**Software change**: services need **shard-aware routing**, through a **client-side algorithm** or a **locator service**
Serve the heavy **seat-map reads** from a **cache** or a **CQRS read model** → the shards spend their capacity on purchases
Use **write-through** for anything that must not be lost

sub: **(1) Hot shards**: one popular event can concentrate writes on one master
**(2) Staleness** of cached or projected seat maps → can show seats as free after they are sold

a.foot: **Cross-shard queries** such as sales reports also get harder.

exam_angles.q: When would you avoid a document store for a new service, and what would you use instead? Give two concrete cases.

sub: Avoid it when the service relies on **joins across many entities**, **multi-record transactions**, or enforced **constraints and triggers**, which most document stores lack
e.g. an **accounting or ledger** service should use a relational store
Avoid it when the data is a **write-heavy stream** of **sparse, timestamped records** read by **key and time range**, where a wide-column store fits better

items: **Also**: when the core queries **traverse relationships** → a **graph** fits
a.foot: A document store **remains a good choice** when an entity and its children are read and written **as one unit** and the **schema keeps changing**.

exam_angles.q: Compare a key-value store and a wide-column store for an IoT platform that writes 50,000 readings a second and reads 'last value for device X' and 'device X over the past week'. Which would you choose, or would you use both?

sub: Answers **'last value for device X'** fastest, as an **in-memory point lookup**
Handles **range queries poorly** and needs a lot of **memory for history**
Serves **'device X over the past week'** well if the **row key** is **device ID plus time**

items: **Defensible design: use both**: **wide-column** for the history + a **key-value cache** for the latest value
**Cost**: writing each reading **twice** and running **two stores**
a.foot: If the last-value query is **rare**, the wide-column store **alone** is enough.

exam_angles.q: Order history is read far more often than it is written, writes go through strict business validation, and the history screens need a different shape from the write model. Design a CQRS solution, and say what users might notice and how you would limit it.

items: **Write side**: commands → a **write API** with full **validation** → a **relational write store**; each committed change **publishes an event**
**Read side**: a **projector** builds a **read model** shaped for the history screens, e.g. **documents** or an **in-memory read store**, served by **read APIs** that **scale independently**
**Users may notice**: not seeing a change they just made, because **projection is asynchronous**
**Limit it**: serve **'my latest order'** from the **write side**, or show it as **pending** until the projection catches up
**Monitor projection lag** and make the projector **idempotent** so replays do not duplicate history
